questions.question: What are the three common tiers of agent memory?
options: Short-term (context window), session memory, and long-term memory
Public memory, private memory, and encrypted memory
Text memory, image memory, and audio memory
questions.explanation: Agent memory is typically architected across three tiers: short-term (the current context window), session memory (persisted across turns within one session, often summarized), and long-term memory (persisted across sessions, typically via retrieval).

questions.question: How is long-term agent memory typically implemented?
options: By storing the entire raw conversation history forever and resending all of it every time
Using the same RAG mechanisms as document retrieval — storing memories as embeddings and retrieving only relevant ones based on the current query
Long-term memory cannot actually be implemented with current technology
By training a brand new model for every user
questions.explanation: Long-term memory faces the same 'don't resend everything' pressure as document retrieval, so it typically reuses RAG mechanisms: storing memories as embeddings and retrieving only the relevant ones for the current context.

questions.question: A user complains that a support agent 'doesn't remember' something from a conversation yesterday. Which question best diagnoses this using the memory tier framework?
options: Should we assume this is a fundamental limitation that can't be fixed?
Is this because we lack long-term memory entirely, or because long-term memory exists but retrieval failed to surface the relevant prior information?
Should we just increase the context window size to fix this?
Is this definitely a hallucination unrelated to memory design?
questions.explanation: This complaint should be diagnosed against the memory tier framework: it distinguishes between having no long-term memory at all versus having it but failing to retrieve the relevant memory, which point to very different fixes.
